title: Avalon Incident Postmortem - Follow-up
summary: Follow-up to the May 28th outage where Avalon saw elevated latencies and KV cache thrashing on Redwood Dedicated. Reviewed root causes (cache eviction under cold-start traffic, autoscaler config gap), mitigations deployed (adjusted autoscaler, added pre-warm warmup job, KV cache tuning), and next reliability improvements and runbooks. Agreed to a pilot of revised autoscaler policy + dedicated warm pools; Redwood to run a 24-hour load test and share logs/graphs. Action items and owners recorded.
topics: Root cause analysis: KV cache & cold starts
Next steps: 24h load test, security docs
next_steps: Redwood to run 24-hour synthetic load test with Avalon traffic profile and share results (Marcus) - target 2027-06-08
Redwood to share updated autoscaler config and recommended warm pool sizing (Jordan) - target 2027-06-06
Avalon to provide representative traffic replay config and SSO test accounts (Maya) - target 2027-06-04
Schedule joint runbook tabletop exercise for incident scenario (Priya to coordinate) - schedule by 2027-06-10
Redwood to send SOC2/ISO audit extract requested by Avalon (Sophie) - target 2027-06-09
action_items: Marcus: run and document 24-hour synthetic load test, include KV cache metrics and latency percentiles - due 2027-06-08
Jordan: prepare autoscaler+warm pool config diff and cost estimate for Avalon Dedicated fleet - due 2027-06-06
Maya: provide traffic replay spec (endpoints, QPS distribution) and test SSO accounts - due 2027-06-04
Priya: set up tabletop exercise invite + pre-read doc and circulate - due 2027-06-07
Sophie: share security package (SOC2, pen test summary, encryption/KMS notes) and updated SLA language - due 2027-06-09
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-06-02 16:00 UTC | Duration: 45 mins | Attendees: Sophie Clarke, Marcus Lin, Priya Patel, Jordan Reyes (Redwood) -- Ethan Zhao, Maya Singh, Luis Romero, Hannah Cole (Avalon)

[00:00] Sophie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you doing this follow-up. We wanted to run through the fixes we pushed after last week's incident and make sure we're aligned on longer term mitigations. Audio's a little choppy on my end, can everyone hear ok?

[00:10] Ethan: Yeah we can hear you. Thanks Sophie. Appreciate Redwood responding quickly, there were some anxious minutes for our oncall.

[00:18] Priya: Hi team -- quick agenda: recap incident, RCA highlights, mitigations applied, proposed reliability improvements, then action items. We'll keep it to 45.

[00:30] Marcus: Quick recap from engineering side: on May 28 we saw a spike in cold-start traffic after a deploy; this triggered autoscaler to spin up new nodes but we observed KV cache thrashing--lots of prefix cache misses--so latency blew up for 95/99th percentiles. We also found the autoscaler cooldown was too aggressive, allowing rapid scale down between bursts.

[00:55] Maya: Right, it looked like our traffic pattern had sharp bursts overnight from our data ingestion pipeline. The platform team didn't expect that cadence and the cache cold start amplified it. Where did the cache eviction policy come from - default?

[01:06] Jordan: Yeah it's largely default LRU-ish behavior in our in-memory KV with a small shard size per pod. Under bursty scale-out, you end up with many tiny caches that can't cover prefixes and the KV miss rate increases. That was exacerbated by our I/O pressure on the node causing GC pauses.

[01:30] Luis: We saw request latency jump from ~40ms p50 to >1.2s p99 for a 20 minute window and error retries from the client spiked. That caused request retries, which fed back into the scaling loop.

[01:45] Marcus: Correct -- cascade effect. Two main root causes: 1) warm pool / pre-warming absent for new nodes so caches start empty, 2) autoscaler policy allowed oscillation plus scale-down too soon.

[02:00] Hannah: From security perspective we were mostly worried about whether any data persisted incorrectly during retries. We validated there were no data exposure issues, right?

[02:10] Sophie: Yes, our post-incident audit shows no PII exposure -- retries were at the application layer, no disk writes of request payloads beyond normal logging. We'll share the audit snippet.

[02:25] Marcus: Mitigations we pushed the same day: increased per-pod cache shard size slightly, turned on a short-lived pre-warm job to populate hot prefixes at scale up, and adjusted autoscaler thresholds to be less sensitive to transient spikes. We also bumped up node I/O priority for the Dedicated pool to reduce GC latencies.

[02:50] Maya: We noticed an improvement in the subsequent window, latency was much better. But curious about the warm pool - how big is it and how much cost impact?

[03:00] Jordan: The warm pool is currently a small reserved set of standby containers that maintain populated KV cache for hot prefixes. For the pilot we recommend 8-12% of average fleet size, which we estimate as roughly a 6-8% cost increase depending on uptime. We'll provide a detailed cost delta.

[03:20] Ethan: That's reasonable if it avoids outages. We care about predictable latency more than marginal cost increases.

[03:30] Marcus: For the longer term, we propose: 1) tune cache eviction to be topology aware (prefer larger shards if node count < X), 2) smarter autoscaler with hysteresis and request-trajectory smoothing, 3) a pre-warm job and optional traffic replay capability so Avalon can seed caches before traffic windows.

[03:55] Luis: Can we get alerts earlier? We want a threshold that triggers before 95th percentiles spike - something like cache miss rate or KV miss ratio.

[04:05] Priya: We can add a per-route alert tied to KV miss > 5% sustained for 2 minutes; Redwood console can push to PagerDuty. We'll draft the recommended thresholds.

[04:20] Marcus: Also want to highlight instrumentation gaps: we didn't have granularity on per-prefix hit rates in the dashboard. Jordan is adding those metrics and a new dashboard panel.

[04:35] Jordan: Yes, adding prefix-level KV hit/miss, per-pod GC pause, and node I/O saturation charts. We'll also surface warm-pool fill rates so you can see readiness during scale events.

[04:50] Hannah: One ask from security: can you document the warm-pool lifecycle and ensure containers don't hold sensitive cached payloads beyond encryption guarantees?

[04:58] Sophie: Definitely -- Jordan will include lifecycle and a TTL for cached entries. Our default ensures encryption at rest for any persisted state and we will not persist request bodies.

[05:12] Ethan: On runbooks -- we need a clear playbook for this incident class. Who does what when latency rises, and an automated mitigation we can trigger.

[05:22] Priya: We're proposing a runbook that starts with auto-scale knobs, then enables warm-pool seeding, and as last resort we failover to a slower but larger model variant to preserve availability. We'll share the draft.

[05:40] Marcus: We should also add a circuit breaker in clients to prevent retry storms during scale events. Avalon could tune retry/backoff too.

[05:50] Maya: We can push a client-side change quickly. We use a 3x retry with fixed backoff currently -- we'll move to exponential jitter.

[06:00] Sophie: Great. Let me run through the agreed immediate actions: Redwood will run a 24-hour synthetic test -- Marcus -- using Avalon's traffic profile to validate warm pool + autoscaler settings; Jordan to produce the autoscaler config diff and cost estimate; Avalon to supply traffic replay config and test SSO accounts; Priya to coordinate tabletop. Anything to add?

[06:20] Ethan: Please include logs/graphs from the May 28 event in the follow-up pack so our execs can see the timeline.

[06:28] Marcus: We'll include the timeline, raw graphs, and KV miss traces.

[06:35] Hannah: And include the security audit snippet Sophie mentioned.

[06:38] Sophie: Yup -- SOC2 extract and summary will be in the packet.

[06:45] Maya: One more question -- you mentioned autoscaler hysteresis; how long before it scales down now? We want to avoid oscillation but also not keep cost forever.

[06:55] Jordan: Current pilot set cooldown to 10 minutes for scale-down and require three consecutive low-util checks to scale down. We can iterate; if it creates too much cost we can tune to 7 minutes. We'll show cost tradeoffs.

[07:10] Luis: Are there any immediate config flags we should flip on our side?

[07:15] Marcus: Nothing required, just provide the traffic replay JSON and SSO test accounts for the replay. We'll handle the rest.

[07:25] Priya: Ok I'm capturing action items now -- Sophie, Marcus, Jordan will send their deliverables. Maya, Ethan, Luis to provide test artifacts.

[07:35] Ethan: Thanks everyone. Overall we felt the response was good, just want assurance this won't repeat.

[07:42] Sophie: Understood. We're treating reliability improvements as priority: warm pools, autoscaler tuning, dashboards, and runbook. We'll loop back after the 24-hour test with detailed results.

[07:53] Marcus: Quick note: during the test we'll also run a variant with and without warm pool so we can quantify cache benefit.

[08:00] Maya: Perfect. When can we expect the results?

[08:05] Marcus: Targeting 2027-06-08 for the test report.

[08:10] Priya: I'll schedule the tabletop exercise for the following week, propose June 14 or 15, and circulate.

[08:18] Sophie: Anything else from Avalon?

[08:20] Hannah: No, that's it. Thanks.

[08:22] Sophie: Great -- recap of next steps in the chat and I'll follow up with the packet. Thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
